preds: Jordan’s Press and Publications Law was amended yesterday in order to restrict the right to freedom of expression on the Internet.
At the same time, journalists and advocates of free expression staged a peaceful demonstration in front of the parliament where the law was being approved.
Carrying a banner reading “Internet Freedom” as their main slogan, advocates for the right to free expression have highlighted the trend toward the death of the Internet in Jordan.
For this proclamation, dubbed the “funeral of the internet,” the protesters wore black clothing.

The approved law still awaits the signature of King Abdullah II, which is required before it can take effect, following the approval of the upper parliament, as is the case for all laws before they come into force in Jordan.
Jemil Nimeri, a member of parliament who opposed the proclamation, not only opposed it but also took part in the protest.
According to them, such proclamations serve only to suppress the voices of the people by restricting freedom.
Website owners are responsible even for the comments their readers post on their websites.
The draft proclamation has sparked strong opposition, and immediately an online campaign was launched with the aim of drawing attention to the uproar it has caused among netizens.
On Twitter, netizens have expressed their frustration in writing.
